article.title: Natural Progress and the Gilded Age: A Review of Our Kindred Creatures
article.author: Rochester Red Star: News from Rochester DSA
article.content: by Travis Covitz Combining my long-standing interest in animal welfare with Gilded Age politics, Our Kindred Creatures: How Americans Came to Feel the Way They Do About Animals by Bill Wasik and Monica Murphy caught my eye at the local library. This 2024 book explores the rise of the American animal welfare movement from the 1860s through the 1890s, looking at pets, livestock, scientific research, wildlife, circuses, and more. Although I was frequently underwhelmed with the politics of the authors, I found this book quite thought-provoking. It is absolutely true that the relationship between the average American and different animals has completely transformed in the past 150 years. Anybody who wants to achieve social change should learn how this came to be. Today the street is considered the place of the car, but it has not always been that way. Our Kindred Creatures starts by asking us to turn back time to the birth of the American industrial city, where the street was shared by man and beast. Stray cats and dogs ran loose, covered in fleas and acting as a constant threat of rabies. Cattle, swine, and more were herded from the farms where they were raised to the butchers who processed them. Horses were, well, the workhorses, moving people, goods, and equipment across the city. Individual acts of cruelty and violence were the norm, not the exception, and Enlightenment philosophy decreed that these animals were unfeeling automatons. To tell the story of American animal welfare, the authors follow three main “heroes” of the movement. All three were white elites in New England. However, rather than leaning into the individualist narrative of social change, the authors consistently demonstrate that these people did not act alone, but used their influential, organized relationships to achieve widely-felt change. The structure of focusing on these three activists serves, rather, to compare and contrast their different tactics in the cause of animal welfare. Henry Bergh was a ‘vigilante’ who used lawfare to protect animals, George Angell was an ‘educator’ who fostered social clubs and magazines for animal welfarists to come together and share ideas, and Caroline White was an ‘innovator’ who helped establish the first animal shelter. Wasik and Murphy highlight the uniting feature of Romantic philosophy, and the other forms of activism these individuals took part in. White was involved in the suffragist movement and Angell became an anti-war advocate. The authors argue that the animal welfare movement came to be as a way for white elites to focus their good will after the success of abolition. The authors themselves relied frequently on emotional appeals and vivid imagery to get their point across. I generally fall pretty evenly on the need for balance between emotion and reason, so I am not inherently opposed to emotion in a political argument, but it did frequently make me so activated that I had to put the book down. Wasik and Murphy clearly have a lot more experience with archives than with animals. They meander between animal welfare and animal rights, in a way that is unclear whether they are staying wholly committed to the Gilded Age context, or they are just that out of touch with modern animal use philosophy. Occasional leaps from the Gilded Age to today feel forced and politicized, rather than a genuine attempt to synthesize history. A phenomenon that I found quite interesting was the way in which anti-welfare politicians made use of the contradictions in animal welfare elitism. For example, labor rights were consistently pitted against the advancement of animal welfare, and some animal welfare legislation was fought specifically on the grounds that it would discriminate against immigrants. Animal welfarists also had a troubled relationship with paternalism and frontier colonialism. The whole concept of animal welfare is, arguably, paternalist in nature, ‘providing a voice for those without one’. Gilded Age animal welfarists who lamented the extinction of the bison saw it as an inevitable part of the march of progress – just as Manifest Destiny was inevitable – and the establishment of national parks, like Yellowstone, were acts of displacing indigenous nations. Wasik and Murphy do try to push back on this paternalism as a mis-step, but they themselves occasionally fall into the trap of valorizing animal ‘innocence’ over human ‘sin’. Despite the difficulties I had with some of the choices of the authors, I did really appreciate how this book sketched out Gilded Age activism. Seeing the way that clashes between Enlightenment ideals and Romanticism, the changing role of religion, and different ideas of ‘progress’ informed what was possible for changemakers was informative and allowed me to think more deeply about our own moment of social upheaval. I do not think this book is especially helpful for someone trying to learn about the animal industry, but it is a great read for someone wanting to learn more about Gilded Age politics.
